messages.subject: Cumulatives
parts:
I pushed a bunch of univariate cumulatives and value tests -- only negative binomial and beta-binomial are missing. One word of caution -- don't trust the binomial or Bernoulli CDFs at the moment as there are likely some compliment issues and off-by-one argument issues I need to sit down and figure out without a sinus headache.

Dan, let me know how you want to proceed with agrad tests and more robust value tests.

-Mike

messages.subject: cumulative doc and notation
parts:
On 12/23/12 1:13 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I pushed a bunch of univariate cumulatives and value tests -- only negative binomial and beta-binomial are missing. One word of caution -- don't trust the binomial or Bernoulli CDFs at the moment as there are likely some compliment issues and off-by-one argument issues I need to sit down and figure out without a sinus headache.

Awesome -- if you send me the LaTeX for the PDF
you sent me before, I can drop it into the manual.

If you'd rather do it yourself, the relevant doc's in

/src/docs/stan-reference/functions.tex

The \fitem{} function defined in stan-manuals.sty formats and
enters a label for the index. I'll probably also be modifying
that file because I'm going to add the binomial_logit parameterization
(and vectorize the gradients in binomial while I'm at it) -- got
sidetracked after looking at the very first BUGS model!

For the manual, is it OK with everyone if we use F(x) for cumulative
distribution functions rather than the P(x) Michael used? I think
we want to say something like:

The cumulative distribution function F(x) for the distribution
Normal(mu,sigma) is

F(x) = Phi((x - mu)/sigma).

Or even F(y) if Andrew feels strongly about his x is for predictors,
y is for variables thing? On p. 25 of BDA, Andrew defines the cumulative
as

F(v_*) = Pr(v <= v_*)

where v is a random variable and v_* a bound variable.

The notational issue is that lower case letters (like v) are overloaded
as random or bound variables in BDA's notation, leading to awkwardness
in translating the usual idiom

If X is a random variable such that X ~ Normal(mu,sigma), then

F_X(x) = Pr(X < x) = Phi((x - mu)/sigma).

I like the BDA notation for applied modeling, as in the Stan modeling language!
It's really clumsy to try to try to capitalize Greek letters, vectors,
matrices, etc.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] cumulative doc and notation
parts:
Yes, I like my notation too! In particular, I think the capital-letter, lower-case letter thing is confusing as it is often used as a way to avoid thinking hard about the fact that y and y.rep have a joint distribution.

The R notation is p (e.g., pnorm, pgamma, etc.), but I'd be happy with F.

And, F(x) is fine. Nothing special about F(y). If anything, I'd write F(theta) to be clear that a distribution does not have to be a data distribution. But I'm happy with F(x).

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] cumulative doc and notation
parts:
On 12/23/12 5:01 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Lemme wait until I'm confident that I have the binomial family correct (and add some more validations), so you only have to change notation in the LaTeX.
OK -- I'll feel free to edit the function doc then.

> On a side note, the negative binomial is written to accept the number of failures as a continuous variable (presumably for over-dispersed modeling) -- is there any reason to extend this to the number of trials in the regular binomial?

Yes, it makes sense to add alternative parameterizations.
I've named them after the transform applied to the regular
parameterization. For instance, right now, I'm working on

binomial_logit(n|N,alpha) = binomial(n|N,inv_logit(alpha)).

I don't think it'd make sense to add it to the cumulative
distribution functions without the corresponding probability
functions, as I think they'll mostly be used to code up
truncation and censoring.

- Bob
